findings.title: W-direction CRC32 confirmed
findings.summary: The 4-byte field at offset 0 of every captured W-direction message is standard zlib CRC32 over (correlation_uuid + envelope), big-endian. Validated 37 of 39 captured W messages.

findings.title: Wire-type-id == typeIndex from runtime registry
findings.summary: info/typeregistry.json (3487 entries) maps each registered type's typeIndex to (uuid, handler, baseVtable). Verified: typeIndex == wire-format type-id. 6 captured types now have authoritative names.

findings.title: Type-id catalog tables are Unicode case-folding
findings.summary: An earlier candidate dispatch table at 0x149f41880 turned out to be the binary's Unicode case-folding lookup, NOT a protocol type-id catalog. The 16960-entry size and the 0x40A→0x45A (Cyrillic Tshe → tshe) mappings gave it away.

findings.title: Cross-codec identity-bundle map (11 sub-systems)
findings.summary: Every captured type's 16-byte identity field decomposes as [sub_system_id:8][session_uuid_lower:8]. 11 distinct sub_system_id values surfaced across the codec library, each tied to a specific message family.

findings.title: Server↔client counter pairs
findings.summary: Four R/W-coupled message pairs documented: 0x18a6↔0x1a59 (counter-coupled 1→2→3→4), 0x15d ping↔ack (verbatim echo), 0x14f R (clock baseline), 0x8e6↔0x9fc (16-byte hash echo).

findings.title: VM-on-Apple-Silicon ruled out for runtime testing
findings.summary: Both UTM and Parallels Desktop fail at GPU detection: paravirtualized GPU presents VendorId=DeviceId=0 to DXGI; the renderer-init rejects. Real-GPU host (AWS g4dn.xlarge or physical Windows) is the next step.

findings.title: Type-name extraction limit + unblock spec
findings.summary: Static-only methodology recovered 5 confirmed captured-type names (REPClient::*, etc.) and 297 of 312 named registry entries. Pushing past 5 captured names needs runtime data — see analysis/typename_unblock_spec.md.

state_machine.name: Init
state_machine.desc: Client object built; nothing on the wire yet.

state_machine.name: DTLS handshake
state_machine.desc: TLS-over-UDP setup. Server cert, key exchange, cipher agreed.

state_machine.name: Connect request
state_machine.desc: Carrier system message asking the server to register the client.

state_machine.name: Connect ack
state_machine.desc: Server acknowledges the connect, opens the data channel.

state_machine.name: V3 registration
state_machine.desc: Client sends its identity (Steam ID, persona, sdk version).

state_machine.name: Registration response
state_machine.desc: Server returns a session token; client validates.

state_machine.name: Heartbeat exchange
state_machine.desc: Ping/ack pair — both sides confirm the session is alive.

state_machine.name: Asset count + key tables
state_machine.desc: Server tells the client what world data to expect.

state_machine.name: World data streaming
state_machine.desc: Bulk world / level data over the chunked stream (0x08).

state_machine.name: Substate setup
state_machine.desc: Open thread — the gate from 10 to 11 is the current blocker.

state_machine.name: World ready
state_machine.desc: Game can render the world; player can move.

state_machine.name: Steady state
state_machine.desc: Heartbeats + world updates only; normal play.

faq.a: A reverse-engineering effort to understand New World's network protocol well enough to build a private server. Right now it's static-analysis work: pulling apart the game binary and a captured login session to figure out how each message on the wire is structured.

Not yet. The codec library can read and re-emit every captured message byte-for-byte, but the runtime side (an actual server you'd point your game at) still needs significant work — at minimum, the connection state machine has an open blocker at the 10→11 transition.

The game runs through a sequence of internal states from "client just started" to "steady gameplay." Our captured replay drives the server through state 10 cleanly, but the predicate that lets state 10 advance to state 11 reads runtime data that the captured replay alone doesn't supply. Cracking that needs a real-GPU host running the game.

faq.q: Is this affiliated with Amazon Games?
faq.a: No. This is an independent reverse-engineering project for research and hobby purposes.

faq.q: Why are some messages "opaque" but others fully decoded?
faq.a: Most captured message types have observable structure (numeric values, known field shapes, repeated patterns) and got full structural codecs. A few (`0x1033`, the largest `0x08`) look like encrypted or signed material — without runtime context we can't subdivide their bodies meaningfully, so the codec just treats them as opaque payloads.

timeline.label: First captured-type codecs ship
timeline.desc: Per-type codecs for the heartbeat, init message, identity beacons, and the subkey-beacon family. Tests grow past 100.

timeline.label: Replay round-trip works
timeline.desc: Full captured DTLS replay parses cleanly. State machine reverse-engineered from binary decompiles; state-10 blocker identified.

timeline.label: Type registry + 5 confirmed names
timeline.desc: 3487-entry runtime type registry mapped against MSVC RTTI strings. 5 captured wire-types confirmed by direct binary match (REPClient::RegistrationResponseMsg, TimeSynchMsg, PingMsg, etc).

timeline.label: Visualization site shipped
timeline.desc: This site! Generated from the codec library + analysis files; deployed to GitHub Pages.

timeline.label: Codec coverage hits 40/40
timeline.desc: Every captured wire-type in the replay now has a codec — including the empty-marker (0x651), the 80-byte frame-config (0x1096), the opaque blob (0x1033), and the chunked stream (0x08, the high-volume world-data type).

timeline.label: Central dispatcher
timeline.desc: Single decode/encode router for every captured type. 174 captured messages round-trip byte-identically through the dispatcher; only documented-edge-case failures remain.
